title: Matrices & Matrix Operations
summary: Matrix multiplication, transpose, inverse, and matrices as linear transformations — the mechanical toolkit everything else in linear algebra builds on.

slides.markdown:
A **matrix** is two things at once: a table of numbers, and a **linear transformation** — a function that moves every point in space in a fixed, consistent way.

A spreadsheet grid and "rotate this image 30°" are the same object viewed differently.

- As a table: rows and columns of numbers you can add, multiply, transpose.
- As a transformation: multiplying a vector by a matrix rotates, scales, or projects it.
- Both views matter — the table view for computation, the transformation view for intuition.

slides.subTitle: Mechanics and dimension rules
slides.markdown:
To multiply `A (m x n)` by `B (n x p)`, each entry of the result is a dot product of a row of `A` with a column of `B`. The result is `m x p`.

The rule to memorize: **inner dimensions must match** (`n = n`) and cancel; the **outer dimensions survive** as the result's shape.

![Matrix multiplication dimension rule](assets/matrix-multiply-dims.svg)

slides.subTitle: Why it isn't commutative
slides.markdown:
`AB ≠ BA` in general — order matters. Take `A` = rotate 90°, `B` = stretch horizontally. Rotate-then-stretch produces a different shape than stretch-then-rotate: the stretch happens along a different axis after the rotation.

Concretely: `A=[[0,-1],[1,0]]`, `B=[[2,0],[0,1]]`. `AB=[[0,-1],[2,0]]` but `BA=[[0,-2],[1,0]]` — different matrices.

This is why in a neural net, layer order genuinely changes the computation — you can't casually reorder matrix operations.

slides.subTitle: Transpose and symmetric matrices
slides.markdown:
The **transpose** `Aᵀ` flips a matrix over its diagonal — row `i` becomes column `i`. `(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ`, note the order flips too.

A matrix is **symmetric** if `A = Aᵀ` — it looks the same reflected over the diagonal. Covariance matrices, adjacency matrices of undirected graphs, and `AᵀA` (always) are symmetric.

Symmetric matrices are special: they always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, which is why PCA relies on them.

slides.subTitle: Identity matrix and inverse
slides.markdown:
The **identity matrix** `I` (1s on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere) is the "do nothing" transformation: `AI = IA = A`.

The **inverse** `A⁻¹` undoes what `A` does: `AA⁻¹ = I`. An inverse exists only if `A` is square and its columns are linearly independent (equivalently, its determinant is nonzero).

Solving `Ax = b` by hand is `x = A⁻¹b` — but in practice you almost never compute `A⁻¹` explicitly; it's numerically expensive and unstable. Solvers use decompositions instead.

slides.subTitle: Determinant
slides.markdown:
The **determinant** measures how much a transformation scales area (2D) or volume (3D and up). `det(A) = 2` means the unit square becomes a shape with twice the area.

A negative determinant means the transformation also **flips orientation** (like a mirror). A determinant of exactly zero means the transformation **collapses** space into a lower dimension — squashing the unit square into a line.

That zero case is exactly when no inverse exists: you can't undo a collapse, since information was destroyed.

slides.subTitle: Singular matrices
slides.markdown:
A matrix is **singular** when `det(A) = 0` — no inverse exists. Practically, this means the transformation throws away information: two different inputs can map to the same output, so you can't reconstruct the input from the output.

This shows up constantly: a features matrix with a duplicated (or exactly collinear) column is singular; a least-squares system with more unknowns than independent equations is underdetermined.

The practical fix is rarely "invert anyway" — it's regularization (ridge) or dropping the redundant dimension.

slides.subTitle: Rotation and scaling example
slides.markdown:
Multiplying every point of the unit square by a matrix `M` rotates and stretches the whole shape in one step — the matrix *is* the transformation, applied uniformly everywhere.

![A matrix as a rotation-and-scaling transformation](assets/rotation-scaling-transform.svg)

This is the model behind graphics pipelines and neural nets: each layer's weight matrix transforms every input vector the same way.

assets.alt: A matrix as a rotation-and-scaling transformation

slides.markdown:
Naively multiplying two `n x n` matrices takes `O(n³)` — for each of `n²` output entries, sum `n` products. At `n = 10,000`, that's a trillion operations.

**Strassen's algorithm** beats this at roughly `O(n^2.807)` by cleverly reusing 7 sub-multiplications instead of 8 for 2x2 block matrices, recursively. It's rarely used in practice below huge `n` — the constant factors and reduced numerical stability outweigh the asymptotic win.

This is the same complexity conversation as sorting or graph algorithms (Area 1 `complexity`) — asymptotics decide what's feasible at scale.
